title: Replace a memory module: release the latches, swap in the new one
instruction: Replace the memory module in slot A2 with the new one from the holder on the right, and stand the old one in the empty holder on the left.
context: Swapping a memory module is a routine PC and server repair. The old module is held by two latches that must both be pressed open before it comes out; the new one only fits one way round and has to be pressed in until both latches click shut.
setup: Left and right are the robot's. Positions are in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Motherboard: an ATX board (305 x 244 mm, 1.6 mm black glass-epoxy PCB with a CPU socket, VRM heatsinks up to 38 mm tall, M.2 heatsinks and expansion slots), lying flat on the table and fixed to it, its long side along x, centred at (0.262, 0.073), so it spans x 0.110 to 0.415 and y -0.049 to 0.195. Its four DDR5 memory slots (black plastic housings, 133 mm long along x, 6.5 mm wide, top 7.8 mm above the table) are centred at x = 0.320 and, from the robot's left, y = 0.010 (A1), 0.000 (A2), -0.010 (B1) and -0.020 (B2). Each slot has a key 6.8 mm from its centre toward +x (away from the robot), and a black plastic latch at each end with a T-shaped press tab on top (8 mm long, 19.8 mm above the table); pressing a tab down and outward tips the latch open. A2's latches are shut; the others' are open. Memory modules (two, identical): DDR5 desktop modules (UDIMM), 133.35 x 31.25 mm green PCB 1.27 mm thick with gold contacts along the bottom edge and a grey aluminium heat spreader on both faces (6.6 mm thick over the spreader, top 34.7 mm above the contact edge), 40 g, key notch 6.8 mm from the centre of the contact edge. The old module is fully seated in A2 with both latches shut on it. The new module stands upright on its contact edge in the right holder, its length along y, with its key notch on the robot's left of centre (toward the board): a quarter turn clockwise, seen from above, puts it the right way round for A2. Right holder: grey plastic block 30 x 150 x 6 mm (x by y) centred at (0.32, -0.19), with two 14 mm wide, 5 mm tall walls along y on top leaving a 2 mm groove. Left holder (empty): grey plastic block 150 x 30 x 6 mm (x by y) centred at (0.32, 0.235), just beyond the board's edge, with two 13.25 mm wide, 5 mm tall walls along x leaving a 3.5 mm groove.
scoring: Judged at the end of the episode from a side photo of the slot, a feeler gauge and a look at the left holder, plus a video of the removal. Torn out: the old module left A2 before both of its latches had been pressed open (in simulation, each latch counts as opened once it is 20 degrees open while the module's end over it is still within 2.5 mm of the slot floor). 0 if the old module was torn out, a module fell off the table, or the old module is still in A2. 0.25: the old module is out of A2. 0.5: and it stands in the left holder's groove, upright within 20 degrees (it may lean on a wall), its length along the groove, released. 0.75: and the new module stands in A2 the right way round (its centre within 1.5 mm of the slot's centre line and centre, within 5 degrees of the orientation that fits the key, upright within 5 degrees, contact edge below the slot's top). 1.0 (success, held for 1 s): and the new module is fully seated (both ends of the contact edge within 0.3 mm of the slot floor) with both latches shut (each within 5 degrees of upright), and both modules are released (no gripper centre within 4.5 cm of either module's middle) and at rest (moved less than 1 mm over the last second). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Take the new module out of A2 (press both latch tabs, pull it out) and stand it in the right holder with its key notch toward the board. Seat the old module in A2 the right way round until both latches click shut. Leave the left holder empty.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz physics, 20 Hz control. The board is fixed. The slot's contacts are modelled as compliant strips that pinch the module's edge; 45-degree lead-ins over the strips and the end guides, and a 0.3 mm bevel on the module's edge, centre a module set down within about 2 mm and 1 degree. Seating takes about 16 N pushed square, less than a real DDR5 socket (up to about 107 N), so the arms can do it. Each latch is a hinged body with an over-centre spring: it snaps shut when the module's end treads its foot; pressing its tab down and outward with about 4 N tips it open and lifts that end 1.8 mm. With a latch shut the module cannot be pulled straight out; forced, it can be torn out, which scores 0. No electrical contact or damage is simulated.
